claim: NogoA inhibits neurite outgrowth of motoneurons (NOM) through interaction with its receptors, Nogo66/NgR.
source: NogoA inhibits neurite outgrowth of motoneurons (NOM) through interaction with its receptors, Nogo66/NgR.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background knowledge about NogoA function.

claim: Inhibition of Nogo receptors rescues NOM, but not to the extent exhibited by NogoA-knockout mice.
source: Inhibition of Nogo receptors rescues NOM, but not to the extent exhibited by NogoA-knockout mice, suggesting the presence of other pathways.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous research and suggests incomplete rescue.

claim: NogoA-overexpressing muscle cells reduced phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (Pgk1) secretion.
source: We found that NogoA-overexpressing muscle cells reduced phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (Pgk1) secretion, resulting in inhibiting NOM.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Reduced Pgk1 secretion from NogoA-overexpressing muscle cells results in inhibiting NOM.
source: We found that NogoA-overexpressing muscle cells reduced phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (Pgk1) secretion, resulting in inhibiting NOM.
evidence: This causal relationship is demonstrated through experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Extracellular Pgk1 stimulates NOM independent of the Nogo66 pathway.
source: Apart from its glycolytic role and independent of the Nogo66 pathway, extracellular Pgk1 stimulated NOM by triggering a reduction of p-Cofilin-S3, a growth cone collapse marker
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing Pgk1 effects independent of Nogo66 signaling.

claim: Extracellular Pgk1 triggers a reduction of p-Cofilin-S3, a growth cone collapse marker.
source: Apart from its glycolytic role and independent of the Nogo66 pathway, extracellular Pgk1 stimulated NOM by triggering a reduction of p-Cofilin-S3, a growth cone collapse marker
evidence: This mechanism is demonstrated through Western blot data in the figures.

claim: p-Cofilin-S3 is a growth cone collapse marker.
source: extracellular Pgk1 stimulated NOM by triggering a reduction of p-Cofilin-S3, a growth cone collapse marker
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about p-Cofilin-S3 function.

claim: p-Cofilin-S3 is a marker of reduced axonal actin dynamics in ALS patients with depleted and mutated C9ORF72.
source: phosphorylated Cofilin at S3 (p-Cofilin-S3), which is a hallmark of growth cone collapse in neuronal cells, as well as a marker of reduced axonal actin dynamics in ALS patients with depleted and mutated C9ORF72 (Heredia et al., 2006; Sivadasan et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Extracellular Pgk1 reduces p-Cofilin-S3 through decreasing a Rac1-GTP/p-Pak1-T423/p-P38-T180/p-MK2-T334/p-Limk1-S323/p-Cofilin-S3 molecular pathway.
source: extracellular Pgk1 stimulated NOM by triggering a reduction of p-Cofilin-S3, a growth cone collapse marker, through decreasing a novel Rac1-GTP/p-Pak1-T423/p-P38-T180/p-MK2-T334/p-Limk1-S323/p-Cofilin-S3 molecular pathway.
evidence: This signaling pathway is demonstrated through experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: The Rac1-GTP/p-Pak1-T423/p-P38-T180/p-MK2-T334/p-Limk1-S323/p-Cofilin-S3 molecular pathway is novel.
source: through decreasing a novel Rac1-GTP/p-Pak1-T423/p-P38-T180/p-MK2-T334/p-Limk1-S323/p-Cofilin-S3 molecular pathway.
evidence: The authors explicitly describe this pathway as novel, indicating it has not been previously reported.

claim: Supplementary Pgk1 enhances NOM in defective cells.
source: Not only did supplementary Pgk1 enhance NOM in defective cells, but injection of Pgk1 rescued denervation in muscle-specific NogoA-overexpression of zebrafish and an Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis mouse model, SOD1 G93A.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data in cell culture experiments.

claim: Injection of Pgk1 rescued denervation in muscle-specific NogoA-overexpression zebrafish.
source: Not only did supplementary Pgk1 enhance NOM in defective cells, but injection of Pgk1 rescued denervation in muscle-specific NogoA-overexpression of zebrafish and an Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis mouse model, SOD1 G93A.
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vivo experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Injection of Pgk1 rescued denervation in an Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis mouse model, SOD1 G93A.
source: Not only did supplementary Pgk1 enhance NOM in defective cells, but injection of Pgk1 rescued denervation in muscle-specific NogoA-overexpression of zebrafish and an Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis mouse model, SOD1 G93A.
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vivo experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Pgk1 secreted from muscle is detrimental to motoneuron neurite outgrowth and maintenance.
source: Thus, Pgk1 secreted from muscle is detrimental to motoneuron neurite outgrowth and maintenance.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the collective experimental findings in the study.

claim: NogoA inhibits neurite outgrowth of motoneurons via Nogo66 and NiGΔ20 domains.
source: NogoA inhibits neurite outgrowth of motoneurons (NOM) via Nogo66 and NiGΔ20 domains (GrandPré et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Pharmaceutical and genetic strategies to ablate known receptors interacting with Nogo66 domain have not successfully reversed inhibited NOM to the extent exhibited by NogoA-knockout mice.
source: Pharmaceutical and genetic strategies to ablate known receptors interacting with Nogo66 domain (Fournier et al., 2001; Atwal et al., 2008; Nakamura et al., 2011) have not successfully reversed inhibited NOM to the extent exhibited by NogoA-knockout mice (Simonen et al., 2003), suggesting the presence of other pathways.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The incomplete rescue by Nogo receptor ablation suggests the presence of other pathways.
source: Pharmaceutical and genetic strategies to ablate known receptors interacting with Nogo66 domain (Fournier et al., 2001; Atwal et al., 2008; Nakamura et al., 2011) have not successfully reversed inhibited NOM to the extent exhibited by NogoA-knockout mice (Simonen et al., 2003), suggesting the presence of other pathways.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited experimental results.

claim: In ALS patients, overexpression of NogoA in muscle was positively correlated with the loss of motor endplates.
source: In Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) patients, overexpression of NogoA in muscle was positively correlated with the loss of motor endplates, and as the presence of NogoA in muscle cells increases, denervation of endplates also increases (Bruneteau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous clinical research.

claim: As the presence of NogoA in muscle cells increases, denervation of endplates also increases.
source: In Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) patients, overexpression of NogoA in muscle was positively correlated with the loss of motor endplates, and as the presence of NogoA in muscle cells increases, denervation of endplates also increases (Bruneteau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous clinical research.

claim: Patients whose NogoA was overexpressed in muscle cells and who were diagnosed with lower motor neuron syndrome (LMNS) had a higher likelihood of progressing to ALS symptoms.
source: It has also been reported that patients whose NogoA was overexpressed in muscle cells and who were diagnosed with lower motor neuron syndrome (LMNS) also had a higher likelihood of progressing to ALS symptoms (Pradat et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous clinical research.

claim: NogoA could be detected in the muscles of mouse embryos at E15 and P1 stages.
source: In a mouse, NogoA could be detected in the muscles of embryos at E15 and P1 stages, but not in the muscles in adults (Wang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: NogoA could not be detected in the muscles of adult mice.
source: In a mouse, NogoA could be detected in the muscles of embryos at E15 and P1 stages, but not in the muscles in adults (Wang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A significant increase of NogoA was found in the muscle fibers of SOD1 G86R mice.
source: Interestingly, a significant increase of NogoA was found in the muscle fibers of SOD1 G86R mice and ALS patients (Dupuis et al., 2002; Jokic et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A significant increase of NogoA was found in the muscle fibers of ALS patients.
source: Interestingly, a significant increase of NogoA was found in the muscle fibers of SOD1 G86R mice and ALS patients (Dupuis et al., 2002; Jokic et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: NogoA-knockout in SOD1 G86R mice (G86R/NogoA-/-) showed longer survival time.
source: NogoA-knockout in SOD1 G86R mice (G86R/NogoA-/-) showed longer survival time and increased survival rate (Jokic et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: NogoA-knockout in SOD1 G86R mice (G86R/NogoA-/-) showed increased survival rate.
source: NogoA-knockout in SOD1 G86R mice (G86R/NogoA-/-) showed longer survival time and increased survival rate (Jokic et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: When NogoA was overexpressed in the muscle of mice, morphological changes of neuromuscular junction (NMJ) were observed.
source: Moreover, when NogoA was overexpressed in the muscle of mice, morphological changes of neuromuscular junction (NMJ) were also observed (Jokic et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Overexpression of Rtn4al (human NogoA homolog) in muscle exhibited an ALS-like phenotype in a zebrafish model.
source: More recently, in a zebrafish model, overexpression of Rtn4al (human NogoA homolog) in muscle exhibited an ALS-like phenotype (Lin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Overexpression of NogoA/Rtn4a in muscle cells may contribute to the etiology of ALS-like disease at an early stage.
source: This line of evidence suggests that overexpression of NogoA/Rtn4a in muscle cells may contribute to the etiology of ALS-like disease at an early stage, even though NogoA could not be detected in the blood (Harel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple cited studies.

claim: NogoA could not be detected in the blood.
source: This line of evidence suggests that overexpression of NogoA/Rtn4a in muscle cells may contribute to the etiology of ALS-like disease at an early stage, even though NogoA could not be detected in the blood (Harel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The molecular mechanism that would explain the association between increased NogoA in muscle cells and the occurrence of neurodegeneration remains largely unclear.
source: However, the molecular mechanism that would explain the association between increased NogoA in muscle cells and the occurrence of neurodegeneration remains largely unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that motivates the current study.

claim: The inhibitory effect of NogoA-overexpressed muscle cells on NOM may be mediated through some secretory myokine released by muscle cells.
source: Therefore, it is a plausible hypothesis that the inhibitory effect of NogoA-overexpressed muscle cells on NOM may be mediated through some secretory myokine released by muscle cells.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis to be tested in the study.

claim: NSC34 cells incubated in Sol8-NogoA CM showed appreciable inhibition of NOM.
source: Next, we incubated mouse motoneuron hybrid NSC34 cells in Sol8-NogoA CM and found appreciable inhibition of NOM.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding demonstrated in Figure 1.

claim: The amount of secreted phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (Pgk1) was dramatically reduced in Sol8-NogoA CM compared to control Sol8 CM.
source: Then, we found that the amount of secreted phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (Pgk1) was dramatically reduced in Sol8-NogoA CM compared to control Sol8 CM.
evidence: This is demonstrated through 2D electrophoresis and Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Upon addition of Pgk1, NOM derived from NSC34 cells cultured in Sol8-NogoA CM was rescued.
source: Upon addition of Pgk1, NOM derived from NSC34 cells cultured in Sol8-NogoA CM was rescued.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Extracellular Pgk1 (ePgk1) reduces the phosphorylation of Pak1/P38/MK2/Limk1/Cofilin axis.
source: Furthermore, we found that extracellular Pgk1 (ePgk1) reduces the phosphorylation of Pak1/P38/MK2/Limk1/Cofilin axis, which, in turn, enhances the NOM in a manner functionally independent from its intracellular, canonical role as a supplier of energy.
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot data in Figure 5.

claim: Extracellular Pgk1 enhances NOM in a manner functionally independent from its intracellular, canonical role as a supplier of energy.
source: Furthermore, we found that extracellular Pgk1 (ePgk1) reduces the phosphorylation of Pak1/P38/MK2/Limk1/Cofilin axis, which, in turn, enhances the NOM in a manner functionally independent from its intracellular, canonical role as a supplier of energy.
evidence: This is demonstrated through glycolysis assay data in Figure 3.

claim: Reduced secretion of Pgk1 from NogoA-overexpressed muscle cells inhibits NOM.
source: Therefore, we conclude that reduced secretion of Pgk1 from NogoA-overexpressed muscle cells inhibits NOM promises a paradigm shift that will inspire new thinking about therapeutic targets against failure NOM and denervated NMJ.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the collective experimental findings.

claim: NogoA was not detected in the CM cultured by Sol8-NogoA cells after Dox induction for 48 hr.
source: Importantly, NogoA was not detected in the CM cultured by Sol8-NogoA cells after Dox induction for 48 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The component(s) contained in CM from cultured Sol8-NogoA play(s) a role in NOM inhibition, but not through NogoA contained in medium.
source: This line of evidence suggested that the component(s) contained in CM from cultured Sol8-NogoA play(s) a role in NOM inhibition, but not through NogoA contained in medium.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that NogoA is not detected in the conditioned medium.

claim: The signal intensity of phosphorylated Cofilin at S3 (p-Cofilin-S3) was upregulated in neurons treated with Sol8-NogoA CM.
source: Moreover, unlike neurons treated with Sol8-vector, Western blot analysis demonstrated that the signal intensity of phosphorylated Cofilin at S3 (p-Cofilin-S3), which is a hallmark of growth cone collapse in neuronal cells, as well as a marker of reduced axonal actin dynamics in ALS patients with depleted and mutated C9ORF72 (Heredia et al., 2006; Sivadasan et al., 2016), was upregulated in neurons treated with Sol8-NogoA CM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The level of Pgk1 protein contained in Sol8-NogoA CM was significantly reduced compared to that in Sol8-vector CM.
source: Among these examined proteins, we found that the level of Pgk1 protein contained in Sol8-NogoA CM was significantly reduced compared to that in Sol8-vector CM (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through 2D electrophoresis and mass spectrometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The degree of p-Cofilin expression in NSC34 cells cultured in CM from Pgk1-overexpressed Sol8-NogoA cells was significantly reduced compared with that in NSC34 cells cultured in CM from Sol8-NogoA cells.
source: Furthermore, the degree of p-Cofilin expression in NSC34 cells cultured in CM from Pgk1-overexpressed Sol8-NogoA cells was significantly reduced compared with that in NSC34 cells cultured in CM from Sol8-NogoA cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data comparing different culture conditions.

claim: The amount of Pgk1 in the sera of SOD1 G93A mice was significantly reduced compared with that in the sera of WT mice.
source: We found that the amount of Pgk1 in the sera of SOD1 G93A mice was significantly reduced compared with that in the sera of WT mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: NogoA is overexpressed in muscle of SOD1 G93A mice.
source: Additionally, we used Western blot analysis to detect the protein level of Pgk1 in the sera of transgenic SOD1 G93A mice, in which NogoA was overexpressed in muscle (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), the results of which were consistent with those reported by Bros-Facer et al. (2014).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot data and supported by citation.

claim: Addition of Pgk1 to Sol8-NogoA CM reduced p-Cofilin-S3 in NSC34 cells.
source: We added Pgk1 directly into Sol8-NogoA CM and found that p-Cofilin-S3 in NSC34 cultured with Sol8-NogoA CM plus Pgk1 was lower than that of cells cultured with Sol8-NogoA CM (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot data in Figure 1A.

claim: Supplementary Pgk1 could reduce p-Cofilin-S3 to then restore NOM of NSC34 cells cultured in Sol8-NogoA CM.
source: Importantly, supplementary Pgk1 could reduce p-Cofilin-S3 to then restore NOM of NSC34 cells, even though they had been cultured in Sol8-NogoA CM, indicating that stalled NOM of NSC34 cells cultured in Sol8-NogoA CM could be rescued upon the addition of Pgk1.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Addition of Pgk1-specific antibody to Sol8-vector CM totally inhibited NOM.
source: To further confirm whether Pgk1 secreted by muscle cells could enhance NOM, we added Pgk1-specific antibody to Sol8-vector CM and then cultured NSC34 cells. In response, NOM was totally inhibited and p-Cofilin-S3 was higher compared to those observed in the control groups, such as Sol8-vector CM and Sol8-vector CM plus rabbit IgG (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data in Figure 1B.

claim: Addition of Pgk1-specific antibody to Sol8-vector CM increased p-Cofilin-S3 compared to control groups.
source: To further confirm whether Pgk1 secreted by muscle cells could enhance NOM, we added Pgk1-specific antibody to Sol8-vector CM and then cultured NSC34 cells. In response, NOM was totally inhibited and p-Cofilin-S3 was higher compared to those observed in the control groups, such as Sol8-vector CM and Sol8-vector CM plus rabbit IgG (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot data in Figure 1B.

claim: Pgk1 is secreted by myoblasts and exists in muscle cell CM to play an important role in enhancing NOM.
source: Thus, we suggest that Pgk1 is secreted by myoblasts and that it exists in muscle cell CM to play an important role in enhancing NOM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antibody blocking experiments.

claim: Pgk1 alone is sufficient to induce NOM and neuronal differentiation.
source: Next, to determine if Pgk1 alone is sufficient to induce NOM and neuronal differentiation, we switched to low trophic factor differentiation media (DM). Under the same condition, Pgk1 was able to extend NOM and downregulate p-Cofilin-S3 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data in Figure 1C.

claim: The effect of adding Pgk1 on the downregulation of p-Cofilin-S3 was dose-dependent from 0, 11, 33, 66 and 99 ng/ml.
source: We also found that the effect of adding Pgk1 on the downregulation of p-Cofilin-S3 was dose-dependent from 0, 11, 33, 66 and 99 ng/ml (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The effect of Pgk1 on the downregulation of p-Cofilin-S3 was time-dependent from 8 through 24 hr.
source: Moreover, when NSC34 cells were treated with Pgk1 at 33 ng/ml for 0, 8, 16, 24 and 48 hr, we found that the effect of Pgk1 on the downregulation of p-Cofilin-S3 was dose-dependent from 8 through 24 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: p-Cofilin-S3 was unexpectedly increased if cells were treated with Pgk1 for 48 hr.
source: However, we noticed that p-Cofilin-S3 was unexpectedly increased if cells were treated with Pgk1 for 48 hr.
evidence: This is an observation from the time-course experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The addition of Pgk1 at 33 ng/ml for 24 hr rescued the number of neurite-bearing cells.
source: Interestingly, the addition Pgk1 at that concentration not only rescued the number of neurite-bearing cells, but also enhanced neurite length of NSC34 cells cultured in Sol8-NogoA CM and DM (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The addition of Pgk1 at 33 ng/ml for 24 hr enhanced neurite length of NSC34 cells cultured in Sol8-NogoA CM and DM.
source: Interestingly, the addition Pgk1 at that concentration not only rescued the number of neurite-bearing cells, but also enhanced neurite length of NSC34 cells cultured in Sol8-NogoA CM and DM (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Syn1 is a marker labeling neuronal synaptic vesicles in cell terminals.
source: To further learn if these restored neurites in NSC34 cells could differentiate into mature neurons, we employed antibody combined with fluorescence staining to specifically detect Syn1, which is a marker labeling neuronal synaptic vesicles in cell terminals (Fletcher et al., 1991), and maturation markers, such as MAP2, GAP43 and ChAT (Maier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: MAP2, GAP43 and ChAT are maturation markers.
source: To further learn if these restored neurites in NSC34 cells could differentiate into mature neurons, we employed antibody combined with fluorescence staining to specifically detect Syn1, which is a marker labeling neuronal synaptic vesicles in cell terminals (Fletcher et al., 1991), and maturation markers, such as MAP2, GAP43 and ChAT (Maier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The percentages of NSC34 cells displaying the Syn1 signal in the growth cones terminal were 43 ± 4.78, 13 ± 1.63 and 45 ± 4.55% in Sol8-vector CM, Sol8-NogoA CM and Sol8-NogoA CM plus Pgk1, respectively.
source: Based on the distribution by immunofluorescence staining against Syn1 within NSC34 cells cultured in CM, the percentages of NSC34 cells displaying the Syn1 signal in the growth cones terminal were 43 ± 4.78, 13 ± 1.63 and 45 ± 4.55% in Sol8-vector CM, Sol8-NogoA CM and Sol8-NogoA CM plus Pgk1, respectively (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence data quantified in Figure 2A-D.

claim: The number of neurons with Syn1 signal at the end of growth cones could be restored to that cultured in Sol8-vector CM after Pgk1 was added in Sol8-NogoA CM.
source: The number of neurons with Syn1 signal at the end of growth cones could be restored to that cultured in Sol8-vector CM after Pgk1 was added in Sol8-NogoA CM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the quantitative data in Figure 2.

claim: The expressions of MAP2, GAP43, Syn1 and ChAT were all increased when Pgk1 was added to the Sol8-NogoA CM/NSC34 culture.
source: We next examined the expression levels of functional proteins, such as MAP2, GAP43, Syn1 and ChAT, in NSC34 cells. The expressions of MAP2, GAP43, Syn1 and ChAT were all increased when Pgk1 was added to the Sol8-NogoA CM/NSC34 culture (Figure 2E), suggesting that Pgk1 addition could rescue weak cell differentiation caused by culturing in Sol8-NogoA CM.
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot data in Figure 2E.

claim: Pgk1 addition could rescue weak cell differentiation caused by culturing in Sol8-NogoA CM.
source: The expressions of MAP2, GAP43, Syn1 and ChAT were all increased when Pgk1 was added to the Sol8-NogoA CM/NSC34 culture (Figure 2E), suggesting that Pgk1 addition could rescue weak cell differentiation caused by culturing in Sol8-NogoA CM.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the increased expression of maturation markers.

claim: Exogenous addition of Pgk1 enables NSC34 cells cultured in Sol8-NogoA CM to improve differentiation, maturation, and neurite growth.
source: Taken together, we conclude that exogenous addition of Pgk1 enables NSC34 cells cultured in Sol8-NogoA CM to improve differentiation, maturation, and neurite growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective data in Figure 2.

claim: Neither the absence nor presence of ePgk1 resulted in any significant difference in glycolytic function of neurons.
source: Since Pgk1 is a key enzyme for glycolysis, it is necessary to determine whether reduced p-Cofilin-S3 and resultant enhancement of NOM by addition Pgk1 could be attributed to glycolytic effect. Neither the absence nor presence of ePgk1 resulted in any significant difference in glycolytic function of neurons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through glycolysis stress test data in Figure 3A.

claim: In low glycolytic condition induced by glycolysis inhibitor 3PO, p-Cofilin-S3 was insignificant compared to the untreated group.
source: Even in the low glycolytic condition induced by glycolysis inhibitor 3-(3-Pyridinyl)−1-(4-pyridinyl)−2-propen-1-one (3PO) (Figure 3B), in which p-Cofilin-S3 was insignificant compared to the untreated group (Figure 3C, lanes 1 vs. 3), ePgk1 still downregulated p-Cofilin-S3 (Figure 3C, lanes 3 vs. 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot data in Figure 3C.

claim: ePgk1 downregulated p-Cofilin-S3 even in low glycolytic condition induced by 3PO.
source: Even in the low glycolytic condition induced by glycolysis inhibitor 3-(3-Pyridinyl)−1-(4-pyridinyl)−2-propen-1-one (3PO) (Figure 3B), in which p-Cofilin-S3 was insignificant compared to the untreated group (Figure 3C, lanes 1 vs. 3), ePgk1 still downregulated p-Cofilin-S3 (Figure 3C, lanes 3 vs. 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot data in Figure 3C.

claim: Addition of Pgk1 mutants, Pgk1-T378P and Pgk1-D375N, both of which lost their catalytic activities, in DM could still reduce p-Cofilin-S3.
source: Moreover, addition of Pgk1 mutants, Pgk1-T378P and Pgk1-D375N, both of which lost their catalytic activities (Lay et al., 2002; Chiarelli et al., 2012) in DM, could still reduce p-Cofilin-S3 (Figure 3D), suggesting ePgk1 promotes NOM independent of glycolysis.
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot data in Figure 3D and supported by citations.

claim: Pgk1-T378P and Pgk1-D375N lost their catalytic activities.
source: Moreover, addition of Pgk1 mutants, Pgk1-T378P and Pgk1-D375N, both of which lost their catalytic activities (Lay et al., 2002; Chiarelli et al., 2012) in DM, could still reduce p-Cofilin-S3 (Figure 3D), suggesting ePgk1 promotes NOM independent of glycolysis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ePgk1 promotes NOM independent of glycolysis.
source: Moreover, addition of Pgk1 mutants, Pgk1-T378P and Pgk1-D375N, both of which lost their catalytic activities (Lay et al., 2002; Chiarelli et al., 2012) in DM, could still reduce p-Cofilin-S3 (Figure 3D), suggesting ePgk1 promotes NOM independent of glycolysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the catalytic mutant experiments.

claim: Muscle-specific knockout of Pgk1 in zebrafish embryos causes defective development of motoneurons.
source: To confirm the role of Pgk1 secreted from muscle cells regulates motoneuron development in vivo, we employed the CRISPR/Cas9 system to knock out Pgk1 in zebrafish embryos. We used muscle-specific α-actin promoter to drive overexpression of Cas9 in muscle cells in order to exclusively knock out the pgk1 gene.
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vivo experiments in zebrafish shown in Figure 4.

claim: Overexpression of Cas9 in muscle cells had no effect on motoneuron development.
source: Compared to control Tg(mnx:GFP) embryos at 30 hpf (Figure 4C), the tRFP signal was observed in the muscle of pZα-Cas9-injected embryos, indicating that Cas9 was overexpressed in certain muscle cells (Figure 4D). Nevertheless, motoneurons were normally developed, which suggests that overexpression of Cas9 in muscle cells had no effect on development.
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging data in Figure 4C-D.

claim: When Tg(mnx:GFP) embryos were coinjected with pZα-Cas9 and pgk1 sgRNA, defective motoneurons were observed.
source: However, when Tg(mnx:GFP) embryos were coinjected with pZα-Cas9 and pgk1 sgRNA, which inhibits the production of Pgk1 in muscle cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), defective motoneurons were observed (Figure 4E), suggesting that the reduction of Pgk1 in muscle cells is followed by impairment of NOM.
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging data in Figure 4E.

claim: The reduction of Pgk1 in muscle cells is followed by impairment of NOM.
source: However, when Tg(mnx:GFP) embryos were coinjected with pZα-Cas9 and pgk1 sgRNA, which inhibits the production of Pgk1 in muscle cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), defective motoneurons were observed (Figure 4E), suggesting that the reduction of Pgk1 in muscle cells is followed by impairment of NOM.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the CRISPR/Cas9 knockout experiments.

claim: Conditional knockout of phosphoglycerate mutase 2 (pgam2) in muscle cells did not affect NOM.
source: In a parallel experiment, by conditional knockout of phosphoglycerate mutase 2 (pgam2) in muscle cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), a downstream enzyme of Pgk1 in the glycolytic pathway, we again confirmed that the glycolysis pathway in muscle did not affect NOM (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging data in Figure 4F.

claim: The glycolysis pathway in muscle did not affect NOM.
source: In a parallel experiment, by conditional knockout of phosphoglycerate mutase 2 (pgam2) in muscle cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), a downstream enzyme of Pgk1 in the glycolytic pathway, we again confirmed that the glycolysis pathway in muscle did not affect NOM (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pgam2 knockout experiments.

claim: Defects in NOM result from a decrease in Pgk1 secretion in muscle cells.
